name: Spain: Madrid, Toledo, Segovia and Salamanca

cities.base: Barrio de las Letras, or Huertas: a walk to the Prado, Retiro, Sol and Atocha for the trains, among the tapas bars, without Malasaña's club noise or Salamanca's prices.
cities.name: Madrid

cities.base: Inside the walls near Zocodover and the cathedral. The point is the old town after dark once the day buses leave, and a hotel outside means climbing back up at night.
cities.name: Toledo

cities.base: The old town between the aqueduct and the Jewish quarter, 10 minutes on foot to the Alcázar and cathedral. The AVE station is 4km out; budget 10 minutes by bus or taxi.
cities.name: Segovia

cities.base: Around Plaza Mayor and the university quarter: everything here is within 15 minutes on foot, and it is the liveliest part of town after dark.
cities.name: Salamanca

places.name: Museo Nacional del Prado
places.note: Velázquez's Las Meninas, Goya's black paintings and Bosch's Garden of Earthly Delights. Monday to Saturday 10:00 to 20:00, Sundays and holidays to 19:00; buy a timed ticket online and skip the free last two hours, when the queue wraps the block.

places.name: Museo Reina Sofía
places.note: Picasso's Guernica is the reason to go. Closed Tuesdays; free evenings and Sunday afternoons have run in past seasons, but reconfirm before you plan a day round them.

places.name: Palacio Real de Madrid
places.note: By floor area the largest working royal palace in Western Europe, about 135,000 sq m, though the royal family lives elsewhere. Closes later in summer and earlier in winter, and shuts for state events with no notice.

places.name: Parque del Retiro
places.note: 125 hectares, free to enter; the two things to actually do are the Palacio de Cristal glasshouse and a rowboat on the pond, about 8 euros for 45 minutes. Sunday mornings bring buskers and crowds round the lake.

places.name: Plaza Mayor
places.note: Built 1619 under Philip III, the king on the horse in the middle; the Casa de la Panadería frescoes are a 1992 repaint. Free and open all hours: walk through, and eat anywhere but the cafés round the edge.

places.name: Mercado de San Miguel
places.note: A 1916 iron-and-glass market reopened in 2009 as 30-plus tapas stands, now over 7 million visitors a year. Graze here rather than plan a meal, and go before 13:00 or after 22:00 to miss the crush.

places.name: Gran Vía and Malasaña walk
places.note: The early-1900s Spanish Broadway of department stores and cinema facades, then 10 minutes north into Malasaña's 18th-century grid of vintage shops and vermouth bars. A street with no gate; shop hours vary, check.

places.name: Templo de Debod
places.note: A 2nd-century BC Egyptian temple, given to Spain in 1968 for its help saving the Nubian monuments from the Aswan Dam. Free, closed Mondays, and the best sunset over the palace in town, so arrive 30 minutes before.

places.name: Matadero Madrid
places.note: A 1920s municipal slaughterhouse turned contemporary arts centre: galleries, a cinema, a design shop and rotating shows. Most exhibitions are free, the crowd is local, and it is closed Mondays.

places.name: El Rastro
places.note: The flea market down Ribera de Curtidores, Sundays and public holidays only: antiques, leather and plenty of tat. Pickpockets work it, so leave the good camera; finish with vermouth in La Latina as it packs up.

places.name: Cerro del Tío Pío
places.note: The Parque de las Siete Tetas, seven grassy mounds with the whole skyline in front of you; locals come just before sunset. 20-plus minutes by metro or bus from Sol. Open ground; hours vary, check.

places.name: Santiago Bernabéu Stadium Tour
places.note: Real Madrid's ground, rebuilt from 2019 with a retractable roof working since 2024 and room for about 85,000. The self-guided tour covers the trophy room, dressing rooms and pitchside; match days shorten or close it, so check the fixtures.

places.name: Sobrino de Botín
places.note: Cuchilleros 17, open since 1725 and the Guinness holder for oldest restaurant; order the wood-oven cochinillo or the lamb. Touristy and dear for what it is, but the oven is the original.

places.name: Casa Labra
places.note: Since 1860, and one order: bacalao croquettes and cod tapas eaten standing at the bar. The PSOE was founded here in 1879, says the plaque. Bring cash and expect a line at the lunch peak.

places.name: La Ardosa
places.note: A centuries-old tavern where Madrileños send their visitors; order the salmorejo with egg and cured tuna and a vermouth from the tap. Small, and standing room at peak hours.

places.name: Santerra
places.note: Its ham croquettes were named the best in the world at Madrid Fusión 2018. A step up in price from the standing bars; book for dinner, and it is closed Mondays.
places.neighborhood: Barrio de Salamanca, Calle General Pardiñas

places.name: Casa Revuelta
places.note: Boneless bacalao fritters a block from Plaza Mayor, lunch service and no dinner most days; closed Mondays. Reportedly cash only, so carry some.

places.name: La Casa del Abuelo
places.note: Since 1906: gambas al ajillo and a glass of the house sweet vermouth. There are several branches now; the Calle Victoria original is the one, small and loud at peak hours.

places.name: Círculo de Bellas Artes rooftop
places.note: The arts club's rooftop, La Azotea, open to anyone for a small entry fee, with the view down Gran Vía at sunset. Expect a line on summer evenings.

places.name: Museo Chicote
places.note: Opened 1931, one of Europe's oldest cocktail bars, where Hemingway, Cortázar and 1960s and 70s film stars drank in a mostly original art deco room. A sit-down cocktail, not a quick stop; dress a notch up.

places.name: Alcázar de Toledo (Museo del Ejército)
places.note: A Roman site, then a 10th-century caliphal fortress, rebuilt for Charles V and Philip II; the 1936 siege left it in ruins and it was rebuilt 1939 to 1957. Now the Army Museum; closed Mondays.
places.neighborhood: Casco Histórico, top of the old town

places.name: Catedral Primada de Toledo
places.note: Gothic, begun 1226, seat of the Primate of Spain, with El Greco's Disrobing of Christ and Goya in the sacristy. Pay for the combined ticket with tower and cloister; morning Mass limits visits.

places.name: Monasterio de San Juan de los Reyes
places.note: Built by Ferdinand and Isabella for their 1476 win at Toro, hung outside with the chains of Christian captives freed in Granada. Come for the cloister, far quieter than the cathedral's.

places.name: Iglesia de Santo Tomé
places.note: One room, one painting: El Greco's 1586 Burial of the Count of Orgaz, still where it was painted to hang. 20 minutes is enough; avoid late morning, when the tour groups come through.

places.name: Sinagoga del Tránsito (Museo Sefardí)
places.note: A 1357 synagogue built for Samuel ha-Levi, treasurer to Pedro I; the Mudéjar ceiling and Hebrew inscriptions survived because it became a church after 1492. Now the national Sephardic museum, closed Mondays.

places.name: Sinagoga de Santa María la Blanca
places.note: Built around 1180 with horseshoe arches and white walls, so inside it reads as a mosque; a church from the 1400s. The oldest synagogue building still standing in Europe, and 30 minutes covers it.

places.name: Mezquita del Cristo de la Luz
places.note: A mosque of 999 to 1000 with its nine vaulted domes intact, one of the very few in Spain not rebuilt as a church. Easy to walk past, and never a queue.

places.name: Mirador del Valle
places.note: The postcard of Toledo wrapped in the Tagus gorge, the view El Greco painted. No footpath from the old town, so take a taxi, a car or the Zocotren, at golden hour or after dark; hours vary, check.
places.neighborhood: across the Tagus gorge, south of the old town

places.name: Museo de Santa Cruz
places.note: A 16th-century hospital behind a Plateresque doorway, holding a small El Greco collection and Toledo archaeology. Free, uncrowded, and the answer to a rainy hour.

places.name: Zocodover and old-town walk
places.note: The main square since Moorish rule, named from the Arabic for livestock market; walk out through the lanes to the cathedral and the Judería. Steep in places, so wear real shoes; hours vary, check.

places.name: Cigarrales and Tagus gorge circular walk
places.note: The path round the gorge below the walls, passing under the Alcántara and San Martín bridges; a local running route, not a coach stop. No shade, so go early or late in summer; hours vary, check.

places.name: Restaurante Adolfo
places.note: The serious sit-down in town, in the Michelin guide though not starred: modern Castilian, a set menu at dinner, marzipan from the family behind a known Toledo marzipan house. Book ahead; closed Sundays.

places.name: El Trébol
places.note: The best-known place for carcamusas, Toledo's own pork and tomato stew, at the bar or on the terrace. Fills fast at lunch with locals and tour groups alike; closed Wednesdays.

places.name: Alfileritos 24
places.note: Castilian cooking in a converted old house: partridge, game and roasts, a step above the bars without Adolfo's prices. Ask for a room with the exposed-beam ceiling.

places.name: La Orza
places.note: A long-running Toledan kitchen in a small art-hung room by the cathedral; order venison, partridge or migas. Shut Sunday nights, and reserve for dinner in high season.

places.name: Bar Ludeña
places.note: A tiny, decades-old bar that locals credit with first serving carcamusas as a tapa; lunch service, standing room, leans to cash. Arrive at opening or wait for a stool; closed Mondays.

places.name: Santo Tomé marzipan
places.note: Toledo's marzipan maker since 1856, sold by weight at the counter; buy the figuritas, the shaped sweets, over the plain bars. Several branches round the old town sell the same thing.

places.name: La Otra Bóveda
places.note: A wine and beer bar with outdoor tables on Calle Sierpe, between Zocodover and the cathedral: a glass once the day buses have gone. Closing days unconfirmed, so check.

places.name: Acueducto de Segovia
places.note: 167 unmortared granite arches, 28.5m at the highest, probably built after 112 AD and carrying water until 1973; UNESCO since 1985. Free and always there; shoot it from the Azoguejo steps at golden hour.

places.name: Alcázar de Segovia
places.note: A royal fortress first recorded in 1120, where Isabella I sheltered in 1474 before her crowning, and a likely model for Disney's Snow White castle. Hours and price not rechecked this year, so confirm, and go at opening.
places.neighborhood: western tip of the old town

places.name: Catedral de Segovia
places.note: The last big Gothic cathedral built in Spain, 16th century, called the Lady of Cathedrals. The cloister and tower cost extra and the tower is worth it for the view to the aqueduct; far quieter than Toledo's.

places.name: Iglesia de la Vera Cruz
places.note: A 12-sided Romanesque church of 1208 tied to the Templars, across the Eresma; the walk over gives the classic Alcázar and cathedral skyline. Closed Mondays; loop it with the Pradera de San Marcos.

places.name: Mirador de la Pradera de San Marcos
places.note: The meadow under the Alcázar's west face, the best angle on the castle and free. A 15 to 20 minute descent and a climb back, so skip it with bad knees; hours vary, check.

places.name: Judería (Jewish Quarter) walk
places.note: The medieval lanes of the Jewish quarter until 1492: find Corpus Christi, a former synagogue, and the mezuzah scars on some doorframes. Quiet even in high season; hours vary, check.
places.neighborhood: old town, south of the cathedral

places.name: Monasterio de El Parral
places.note: A 15th-century Hieronymite monastery with a few monks still in residence, so visits are mornings in most seasons. Free, and you will likely have it to yourself; closing days unconfirmed, check.
places.neighborhood: across the Eresma, north of the Alcázar

places.name: Real Casa de la Moneda
places.note: The 16th to 17th century royal mint, one of Europe's first industrial ones, now a free coin-making museum and the aqueduct interpretation centre. Short hours, 10:00 to 14:00, and closed Mondays.
places.neighborhood: below the aqueduct, by the Eresma

places.name: La Granja de San Ildefonso
places.note: The 18th-century Bourbon summer palace modelled on Versailles, 20 minutes by bus. The fountains are the reason to go and run on a limited seasonal schedule, so check before you ride out; closed Mondays.

places.name: City walls and Puerta de Santiago walk
places.note: Stretches of the medieval wall and gates round the old town edge, no signs and no tour; the evening loop once the day-trip buses clear out. Hours vary, check.

places.name: Mesón de Cándido
places.note: Since 1884 at the foot of the aqueduct, the town's famous cochinillo house; the show is the pig carved with the edge of a plate. Tour groups fill lunch, so book or take an early or late seating.

places.name: Restaurante José María
places.note: The other big cochinillo name, off Plaza Mayor, run by a chef who has pushed Segovia's suckling pig as a protected dish; the judiones, giant local beans, are good too. As tour-group heavy as Cándido.

places.name: Mesón Duque
places.note: Billing itself as Segovia's oldest inn, from 1895; a third cochinillo house for when you want the dish without the wait at Cándido or José María.

places.name: La Cocina de San Millán
places.note: Smaller and more modern Castilian cooking, the lunch off from roast pork, served 13:00 to 16:00. Closed Mondays and Tuesdays in most seasons, so check before you plan round it.
places.neighborhood: San Millán, edge of the old town

places.name: Limón y Menta
places.note: The counter for ponche segoviano, the town's marzipan and custard sponge, made here since the early 1900s by most accounts. Buy a slice, not the whole cake, and eat it standing.

places.name: El Bernardino
places.note: A traditional roast-meats house near the cathedral, better known to locals than to visitors. The fallback for cochinillo when Cándido and José María are full.

places.name: Bar Rubi
places.note: Craft beer and tapas on Calle Escuderos, a minute from Plaza Mayor and the cathedral, for the evening after the buses leave. Closing days unconfirmed, so check.

places.name: El Secreto de San Clemente
places.note: A restaurant-bar whose outdoor terrace faces the aqueduct head on: an evening drink with the arches in front of you. Closing days unconfirmed, so check.

places.name: Plaza Mayor de Salamanca
places.note: Golden sandstone Baroque, built 1729 to 1755, with stone medallions of kings and later figures round the arcade. Free and open all hours; sit for the view once, and eat elsewhere.

places.name: Universidad de Salamanca (Escuelas Mayores)
places.note: Founded 1218 by Alfonso IX, the fourth-oldest university in continuous operation. Students hunt the tiny carved frog on a skull in the Plateresque facade for exam luck; bring a zoom lens, it is small and high.

places.name: Catedral Nueva y Vieja de Salamanca
places.note: A Romanesque Old Cathedral and a Gothic-Baroque New one, joined inside; find the astronaut and the dragon eating ice cream, 1990s restorers' jokes. The Ieronimus tower climb is a separate ticket and worth it.

places.name: Casa de las Conchas
places.note: A late-15th-century house studded with about 300 carved scallop shells, the Order of Santiago's badge; now a public library, free to enter the courtyard. Five minutes on the way to the university.

places.name: Puente Romano and Río Tormes walk
places.note: A 1st-century Roman bridge still carrying walkers over the Tormes, with the stone verraco boar from Lazarillo de Tormes at its foot. The far bank has the best view of the cathedral towers; hours vary, check.

places.name: Convento de San Esteban
places.note: A Dominican monastery with a Plateresque facade and a gilded Churrigueresque altarpiece, where the friars reportedly weighed Columbus's plans. Quieter than the cathedral next door.

places.name: Huerto de Calixto y Melibea
places.note: A small free garden on the old wall above the river, named for the lovers of La Celestina; the river and cathedral view without the walk down. Tucked behind the cathedral and easy to miss.
places.neighborhood: behind the cathedral, above the Tormes

places.name: Museo Art Nouveau y Art Déco (Casa Lis)
places.note: A 1905 glass-and-iron modernist house full of Art Nouveau and Art Deco: Lalique glass, dolls, fans. A break from Renaissance stone, and rarely crowded.
places.neighborhood: old town, by the river wall

places.name: Palacio de Monterrey (exterior)
places.note: A 16th-century Renaissance palace still owned by the House of Alba, seen from outside except on rare open days; the turreted roofline is the picture. Free from the street; hours vary, check.

places.name: Torre del Clavero
places.note: A free-standing 15th-century octagonal defence tower, one of the last in the city; exterior only, free, and two minutes off the university walk. Hours vary, check.

places.name: Restaurante Víctor Gutiérrez
places.note: Salamanca's Michelin-starred table: Peruvian technique on Castilian produce, as a tasting menu. Book well ahead and reconfirm the days, since it is closed Sundays and Mondays in most seasons.

places.name: La Cocina de Toño
places.note: Creative modern-Castilian tapas and small plates, Bib Gourmand in past guides, somewhere between a bar and a tasting menu. This year's Michelin status unconfirmed; closed Mondays.

places.name: Mesón Cervantes
places.note: Tapas above Plaza Mayor: take the upstairs terrace looking straight down on the square and pay the premium, because the ground-floor tapas are ordinary. A first-night meal, not a locals' pick.

places.name: Doctor Cook
places.note: Playful, kitchen-forward small plates instead of the jamón and croquetas standards, with a younger local crowd. Closed Mondays in most seasons.

places.name: Tapas 2.0
places.note: Modern tapas on Calle Felipe Espino in the university quarter, named in current Salamanca tapas roundups. Hours and closing days unconfirmed; hours vary, check.

places.name: Mercado Central charcuterie counter
places.note: The jamón ibérico and cheese counter in the working market behind Plaza Mayor; try Guijuelo ham from down the road by the slice. Go in the morning, when the market is busy; closed Sundays.

places.name: iPan iVino
places.note: A wine bar on Calle Felipe Espino, a separate door from Tapas 2.0, with a long wine list and small plates. Hours and closing days unconfirmed; hours vary, check.

destination.name: Spain: Madrid, Toledo, Segovia and Salamanca
destination.pitch: Madrid for the Prado and the tapas bars, then Toledo, Segovia and Salamanca by fast train, a night or two each so you see them after the day-trip buses leave. A week, and not in August.
destination.caveat: August runs past 40°C in Toledo and Salamanca, and many small Madrid restaurants shut for the month. Toledo and Segovia fill with tour buses from 10:00 to 17:00. Reina Sofía closes Tuesdays, and Segovia's AVE station sits 4km out of town. Put together for you just now from a live search, so check anything you're pinning the trip on.

because.city: Madrid's Retiro, Malasaña and a Sunday at El Rastro, cocktails at Museo Chicote, the Bernabéu tour, and Salamanca's Plaza Mayor filling up at night in a town of 30,000 students.
because.food: Bacalao croquettes at Casa Labra, gambas at La Casa del Abuelo, cochinillo from Botín's 1725 oven and at Cándido, carcamusas at Bar Ludeña in Toledo, and Guijuelo ham by the slice in Salamanca's market.
because.culture: Las Meninas at the Prado, Guernica at the Reina Sofía, El Greco's Count of Orgaz in Santo Tomé, Toledo's synagogues and its 999 mosque, Segovia's Roman aqueduct and an 800-year-old university in Salamanca.
because.exploration: Sunset with locals on the Cerro del Tío Pío, the gorge path round Toledo, El Parral monastery with nobody else in it, and the Eresma meadow under Segovia's Alcázar.
